---
title: "Install R (and optionally Python or Rust)"
---

The course is taught in **R**: install it first. The exercises also show every code
example, hint and solution in **Python** and **Rust**, so if you prefer one of
those you can work the exercises in it; install it as well in that case.

## R

1. Install a recent [R](https://cran.r-project.org/) (4.3 or newer) from CRAN.
2. We recommend [RStudio Desktop](https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/) as editor.
3. Install the packages used in the course:

```r
install.packages(c(
  "tidyverse",   # data wrangling and plotting
  "Matrix",      # dense and sparse matrices (ships with R)
  "deSolve",     # ordinary differential equations (Part 8, Part 11)
  "rootSolve",   # steady states of ODE models (Newton for systems, phase plane)
  "numDeriv",    # numerical gradients, Jacobians and Hessians (Parts 7 and 10)
  "irlba",       # a few singular vectors of a big matrix (eigen algorithms)
  "RSpectra",    # a few eigenvalues of a big sparse matrix (eigen algorithms)
  "nnls",        # non-negative least squares (SVD and deconvolution)
  "minpack.lm",  # Levenberg-Marquardt fitting (nonlinear least squares)
  "lpSolve",     # linear programming (flux balance analysis)
  "pracma"       # textbook numerical methods (for comparison)
))
```

## Python (optional)

1. Install Python 3.11 or newer, e.g. via [Miniforge](https://github.com/conda-forge/miniforge).
2. Any editor works; [VS Code](https://code.visualstudio.com/) and
   [JupyterLab](https://jupyter.org/) are common choices.
3. Install the packages used in the course:

```bash
pip install "scipy>=1.15" numpy matplotlib pandas
```

## Rust (optional)

1. Install Rust with [rustup](https://rustup.rs/).
2. Get the course's Rust project, which contains every Rust solution as a
   runnable example, from the
   [course repository](https://github.com/henriksson-lab/course_numericanalysis)
   (folder `rust/`), and build it once to download the crates:

```bash
cd rust
cargo build --examples
cargo run --example install_check
```

## Check it works

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

### R

```r
A <- matrix(c(2, 1, 1, 3), nrow = 2)
b <- c(1, 2)
solve(A, b)          # should print 0.2 0.6
0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3     # FALSE: see How computers store numbers
```

### Python

```python
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[2.0, 1.0], [1.0, 3.0]])
b = np.array([1.0, 2.0])
print(np.linalg.solve(A, b))   # should print [0.2 0.6]
print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)        # False: see How computers store numbers
```

### Rust

```rust
// rust/examples/install_check.rs
use nalgebra::{matrix, vector};

fn main() {
    let a = matrix![2.0, 1.0;
                    1.0, 3.0];
    let b = vector![1.0, 2.0];
    let x = a.lu().solve(&b).unwrap();
    println!("{:?}", x.as_slice());   // should print [0.2, 0.6]
    println!("{}", 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3); // false: see How computers store numbers
}
```

:::

If that prints without error, you are ready for the course!
